Analytic Function. An analytic function is a function that can be locally represented by a convergent power series—specifically, a Taylor series. While real analytic functions are infinitely differentiable, complex analytic functions, also called holomorphic functions, have a remarkable property: a single complex derivative guarantees infinite differentiability and analyticity. This rigidity makes analytic functions central to complex analysis, number theory, and mathematical physics.

Formally, a function f is analytic at a point x naught if it can be expressed as a power series: f of x equals the sum from n equals zero to infinity of a-sub-n times the quantity x minus x-naught to the power n, where this series converges to f of x for all x in some neighborhood around x naught.

Here's a key distinction: the class of all real analytic functions on a domain is strictly smaller than the class of infinitely differentiable functions. Real analytic functions are denoted C-omega, which is a strict subset of C-infinity. For instance, consider the function that equals e to the negative one over x squared for x not equal to zero, and zero at x equals zero. This function is infinitely differentiable but not analytic at the origin—its Taylor series converges to zero, yet the function itself is positive everywhere else nearby.

In complex analysis, analyticity is equivalent to being holomorphic, meaning complex-differentiable on an open set. The Cauchy-Riemann equations provide the test: a complex function f of z equals u of x, y plus i times v of x, y is analytic if and only if its real and imaginary parts satisfy specific partial differential equations.

Several deep theorems reveal the rigidity of analytic functions. The Identity Theorem states that if two analytic functions on a connected domain agree on a subset with an accumulation point, they must agree everywhere on the domain. Liouville's Theorem says any bounded, entire function—analytic everywhere in the complex plane—must be constant. These theorems show that analytic functions are highly constrained by their values on small sets.
